notes.meaning: Jacob settled in Canaan, the land where his father Isaac had lived as a foreigner. Like Abraham and Isaac, he lived there as a traveler. He did not yet own the land. He trusted God's promise that it would one day belong to his family. Matthew Henry adds a gentle lesson: we are never fully at home until we reach heaven.

"The account of Jacob" means the story of what happened to Jacob's family, not just a list of names. Joseph was seventeen. Though he was his father's favorite, he was not raised to be lazy. He worked as a shepherd beside his half-brothers. Most older writers say Joseph told his father about his brothers' wrong behavior so that Jacob could correct them, not to stir up trouble. Calvin and the Geneva notes think instead that Joseph complained about how the brothers mistreated him.

Jacob loved Joseph most. Joseph was the first son of his dear wife Rachel, born when Jacob was old. Some older readings take "son of his old age" to mean a wise son, old beyond his years. The special robe was a mark of honor, perhaps hinting at greater honors to come. Keil and Delitzsch think it was a long robe with sleeves, the kind nobles wore. The commentators agree that Jacob was unwise to show such open favoritism among his sons.

The brothers saw their father's favoritism and hated Joseph for it. They would not even greet him with the usual friendly greeting, "Peace to you." Holding back that greeting was a clear sign of ill will. Matthew Henry notes that when parents play favorites, children notice quickly, and families quarrel.

Joseph had a dream and told his brothers, and they hated him even more. Older writers see this dream as God showing Joseph what would come. Joseph had many hard years ahead. Wesley and Matthew Henry say God gave him this early glimpse of his future to comfort and steady him through his troubles.

In the dream, the brothers' bundles of grain bowed down to Joseph's bundle. The picture fits what later happened. Years later the brothers came to Egypt to buy grain from Joseph and bowed before him. Matthew Henry puts it simply: their empty bundles would bow to his full one.

The brothers understood the dream correctly, but they scorned it. How could the younger one rule over the older many? The Geneva notes say that the more God shows favor to his own, the more the wicked rage against them. Matthew Henry and Wesley compare this to people who refuse to let Jesus rule over them.

In the second dream, the sun, moon, and eleven stars bowed to Joseph. They stand for his father, his mother, and his eleven brothers: the whole family. The dream came a second time with a new picture. That repetition showed the matter was sure to happen.

Jacob scolded Joseph, probably to calm the angry brothers. Inside, he took the dream more seriously than he let on. Rachel had already died, so Jacob may have been hinting that the dream was impossible. Matthew Henry and Calvin say the sun and moon simply stand for the heads of the whole household. Calvin adds that Jacob should not have pretended to dismiss something that might be from God.

The brothers grew jealous, but Jacob kept thinking about the dream. He was much like Mary, who treasured things about Jesus in her heart. The Geneva notes say Jacob sensed God was behind the dream, even though he did not yet understand it. He no doubt remembered it years later when it came true.

The brothers took the flocks about fifty miles north to Shechem, where the grass and water were rich. Shechem was also where some of them had once killed the men of the city. So the area could be dangerous for them.

Jacob sent Joseph to check on his brothers and the flocks. He may have worried that their neighbors would take revenge for the killings at Shechem. Joseph answered, "I am ready," even though he knew his brothers hated him. Matthew Henry sees a picture of Christ here: a loving father sends his beloved son to people who will plot against him.

Joseph could not find his brothers at Shechem. A stranger told him they had gone on to Dothan, a little farther north. Joseph could have gone home, but he kept searching until he found them. Matthew Henry and Calvin say this shows real love for his brothers. It also makes their cruelty even worse.

The brothers saw Joseph far off and planned to kill him before he even arrived. This was not a sudden burst of anger. It was cold, planned hatred. Matthew Henry recalls 1 John 3:15: whoever hates his brother is a murderer. The Geneva notes add that the Bible does not hide the sins of its heroes.

"That dreamer" is literally "master of dreams," a bitter sneer. The brothers planned to kill Joseph and hide it with a lie about a wild animal. They thought that would end his dreams. But the commentators note that people cannot defeat God's plans. Calvin says God always finds a way to do what he has decided.

As the oldest son, Reuben had the most reason to resent Joseph, yet he became his best friend here. He talked the others into throwing Joseph into a dry well instead of killing him. He secretly planned to rescue him later. He may also have hoped to win back his father's favor. Calvin notes that leaving Joseph to starve in a pit was still terribly cruel.

The brothers tore off the special robe, the hated sign of their father's favor. Matthew Henry pictures them mocking Joseph as they did it. He compares it to Jesus being stripped of his robe. Adam Clarke suggests they also wanted Joseph to look like an ordinary person, so no one would ask about him.

They threw Joseph into an empty, dry pit to die of hunger and cold. Later the brothers admitted that Joseph had begged them for mercy (Genesis 42:21). The Geneva notes say they fooled themselves. They thought it was not murder if they shed no blood.

While Joseph cried in the pit, his brothers calmly sat down to eat. The commentators see a hardened conscience, with no sorrow at all. Just then a trading caravan came by. It carried spices that were in high demand in Egypt, often for preparing the dead. Matthew Henry sees God's quiet guidance in its timing.

Judah asked what they would gain by killing their own brother, and he suggested selling Joseph instead. Calvin sees a little humanity returning. Judah admits that letting Joseph die would still be murder before God. Keil and Delitzsch add that Judah still wanted Joseph gone so the dreams could not come true. Matthew Henry's lesson: when tempted, remember that sin brings no real profit.

The traders are called both Ishmaelites and Midianites. Many older writers say it was one mixed caravan of Arab merchants, so the names were used for the same group. The price was twenty shekels of silver, later the set value of a boy (Leviticus 27:5). Matthew Henry and Wesley note that Judah sold Joseph for twenty pieces, and Judas sold Jesus for thirty.

other.label: Modern scholarship
other.view: Some scholars think the different names for the traders show the story was put together from more than one older account.

notes.meaning: Reuben had been away, maybe circling back to rescue Joseph in secret. He found the pit empty and tore his clothes in grief. As the oldest, he knew his father would hold him responsible. Matthew Henry points out that if Reuben's plan had worked, God's bigger plan for Joseph in Egypt would not have happened.

To hide one sin, the brothers committed another. They dipped the robe in goat's blood and sent it to their father. Then they asked him whether it was his son's robe. Matthew Henry and Adam Clarke see deliberate cruelty in this. Calvin thinks servants may have carried the robe, so the brothers would not be suspected.

Jacob knew the robe at once and assumed the worst: a wild animal had torn Joseph apart. Adam Clarke suggests the robe may also have been ripped, which made the lie more believable. Matthew Henry notes that love quickly fears the worst. He adds that Jacob may also have blamed himself for sending Joseph alone.
Jacob tore his clothes and wrapped rough sackcloth around his waist. These were common signs of mourning in that part of the world. He grieved for a long time.

"Daughters" may include his sons' wives, since Jacob had only one daughter, Dinah. The sons pretended to comfort him, though one word of truth would have helped. Jacob said he would go to Sheol, the place of the dead, still mourning. Matthew Henry and Wesley warn that clinging too tightly to anything we love leads to grief that is too heavy. Calvin thinks Jacob refused human comfort but still bowed to God.

Meanwhile Joseph was sold again in Egypt to Potiphar, a high royal official and captain of Pharaoh's bodyguard. Calvin says that even as Joseph passed from hand to hand, God never stopped caring for him. Matthew Henry traces the chain that followed: Israel went down to Egypt, was later rescued by Moses, and in time the gospel went to all nations. Many older writers see Joseph as a picture of Christ, humbled first and then raised up. Adam Clarke and Keil and Delitzsch warn not to push every detail too far.
